country.name: Oregon
country.summary: Oregon is the Pinot Noir state. Its modern industry began in 1961 with Riesling in the Umpqua Valley and found its calling in 1965, when The Eyrie Vineyards planted Pinot Noir in the Willamette Valley against the advice of the day. Pinot Noir is by far the most planted grape, Pinot Gris leads the whites, and the Willamette Valley holds most of the acreage and nearly all of the reputation. Southern Oregon, the Umpqua and Rogue valleys, is warmer and grows Syrah, Tempranillo and Bordeaux varieties; the Columbia Gorge, the Columbia Valley, the Walla Walla Valley and the Snake River Valley cross the state line and are shared with neighbours. Oregon's label law is the strictest of any American state, and the exam asks it: 90 per cent of the named grape, 95 per cent from a named AVA, every grape from Oregon when the label says Oregon.
country.overview:
Oregon came late and small. The nineteenth century had a few vineyards in the Rogue Valley and around Salem, Prohibition erased them, and nothing of consequence returned until Richard Sommer planted HillCrest Vineyard near Roseburg in 1961, mostly to Riesling. The turn that made the state came four years later: David Lett, trained at Davis and told that Pinot Noir would never ripen in Oregon's rain, planted it anyway in 1965 and settled The Eyrie Vineyards in the Dundee Hills in 1966. A handful of families followed within six years, among them the founders of Erath, Ponzi, Adelsheim and Sokol Blosser, all planting Pinot Noir on the hillsides north and west of Salem. Eyrie's 1975 South Block Reserve placed among the best Pinot Noirs at a Paris tasting in 1979, held its place in a rematch against Burgundy the next year, and the house of Joseph Drouhin answered by buying Dundee Hills land in 1987 for Domaine Drouhin Oregon. The valley's first traditional-method sparkling house, Argyle, opened in Dundee the same year.

Geography is two mountain ranges and the valleys between. The Coast Range takes the first weight of Pacific weather; the Cascades, further inland, hold back the continental extremes of the east. Between them lies the Willamette Valley, cool and wet in winter, dry in summer, which is why Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and Chardonnay suit it. South of the Calapooya Mountains the Umpqua and Rogue valleys are warmer, drier and more broken, and the Applegate Valley sits inside the Rogue; they ripen Syrah, Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, and Southern Oregon is the umbrella AVA over both. East of the Cascades, Oregon's share of the Columbia Gorge, the Columbia Valley and the Walla Walla Valley is desert country shared with Washington, and the Snake River Valley is shared with Idaho. The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater, approved in 2015, lies wholly in Oregon yet inside the Walla Walla Valley, which is why its Syrah is spoken of with Washington's.

The law has three floors above the federal one. In 1977 Oregon forbade generic names such as Burgundy and Chablis on its labels and set the varietal minimum at 90 per cent, where federal law asks 75; a listed group of grapes that are blended by tradition, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Tempranillo and the other Bordeaux and Rhône varieties among them, may still be labelled at 75. A wine that names an Oregon AVA must hold 95 per cent from it, and a wine that says Oregon must be Oregon grapes entirely. A statute of 2019, in force for labels from 2023, requires the words Willamette Valley beside any of the valley's nested AVA names. None of this ranks a vineyard: an AVA says where, never how good.

The exam leans on the Willamette Valley and its nested AVAs, the Jory and Willakenzie soils, the Van Duzer Corridor, the 1965 founding, Drouhin's arrival, the 90 per cent rule against the federal 75, and the Rocks District's odd address.
ladder: A label that says Oregon must be made from Oregon grapes alone; federal law would allow 75 per cent for a state name.
An Oregon county on the label, such as Yamhill County, holds Oregon to the same 95 per cent rule it applies to an AVA.

A federally delimited area, origin only: Willamette Valley, Umpqua Valley, Rogue Valley, Southern Oregon, and the shared Columbia Gorge, Columbia Valley, Walla Walla Valley and Snake River Valley. Oregon asks 95 per cent from a named AVA that lies within the state; federal law asks 85.

An AVA inside another: the Willamette Valley's eleven, Applegate Valley within Rogue Valley, Elkton Oregon and Red Hill Douglas County within Umpqua Valley, The Rocks District within Walla Walla Valley. A Willamette nested name must stand beside the words Willamette Valley.
A named vineyard on the label is a house's own claim, not a legal tier; the AVA rules still apply to the grapes.
No legal meaning in Oregon or anywhere in the United States; a house's own word.
labels: The AVA of 1983 between the Coast Range and the Cascades; the word that must stand beside any nested AVA name.
The nested AVAs a server meets most, named after the hills and towns north-west of Salem.
The federal term: every grape from vineyards the winery owns or controls inside the named AVA, the wine made and bottled on the premises.
Oregon's leading white, nearly always labelled Gris rather than Grigio, usually dry and unoaked.
Dry traditional-method sparkling wine from Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sometimes Meunier; Argyle made the style at home in Dundee from 1987.
The umbrella AVA over the Umpqua and Rogue valleys, warmer country for Syrah, Tempranillo and Bordeaux grapes.
The Pacific Northwest's sustainability certification for vineyards and wineries, begun among Oregon growers in the late 1990s.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: By far the most planted grape: red-fruited, earthy, silky wine from the Willamette Valley, the reason Oregon is on the exam at all.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: The leading white, first planted by Eyrie in the 1960s; dry, pear-scented and fuller than Italian Grigio, nearly always unoaked.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Lean and mineral since the Dijon clones replaced the late-ripening Californian selections; barrel-fermented in the Burgundian manner.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: The grape of the state's first modern vineyard in 1961; dry to off-dry wines from the cooler sites.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Southern Oregon's red, peppery and dark in the Rogue and Umpqua valleys, and savoury on the cobbles of The Rocks District.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: A Southern Oregon success in the Umpqua and Rogue valleys, where the heat Pinot Noir dislikes ripens it well.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.styles: A small but growing Willamette planting for bright, crunchy reds in the Beaujolais manner.

exam: Hold the three Oregon floors: 90 per cent varietal, 95 per cent from a named AVA, 100 per cent Oregon for a state label.
Know the exceptions at 75 per cent by family: Cabernet Sauvignon and the Bordeaux grapes, Syrah and the Rhône grapes, Tempranillo, Zinfandel.
Name the founding dates: HillCrest 1961, Eyrie 1965, Willamette Valley AVA 1983, Domaine Drouhin Oregon 1987.
Place the shared AVAs: Columbia Gorge, Columbia Valley and Walla Walla Valley with Washington, Snake River Valley with Idaho.
Keep Southern Oregon apart from the Willamette: warmer, drier, Syrah and Tempranillo rather than Pinot Noir.
Say the state's name as a native does, OR-ih-gun, never or-ih-GONE.
traps: The 90 per cent rule is Oregon's, not federal law; Washington and New York follow the federal 75.
Cabernet Sauvignon in Oregon may be labelled at 75 per cent; Pinot Noir may not.
The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater is in Oregon, inside the Walla Walla Valley AVA, and a wine finished in Washington may not put the district's name on its label.
Columbia Gorge and Columbia Valley are two different AVAs, both shared with Washington; the Gorge is not inside the Valley.
Oregon's first modern vineyard was HillCrest in the Umpqua Valley, Riesling in 1961, not Eyrie; Eyrie was the first Willamette Pinot Noir.
Oregon grows little Zinfandel and almost no Cabernet Sauvignon in the Willamette; those are California and Washington stories.

questions.q: Which Oregon vineyard, planted in 1961 in the Umpqua Valley, began the state's modern wine industry?
questions.exp: HillCrest near Roseburg was planted in 1961, mostly to Riesling. Eyrie, Ponzi and Sokol Blosser are Willamette Valley pioneers of 1965 to 1971.

questions.q: What minimum share of grapes must come from a named Oregon AVA under state law?
questions.exp: Oregon asks 95 per cent from the named AVA, above the federal 85. The 100 per cent rule applies to a label that says Oregon.

questions.q: Which AVA lies wholly in Oregon yet sits inside the Walla Walla Valley AVA?
questions.exp: The Rocks District, approved in 2015, is the cobbled alluvial fan of the Walla Walla River on the Oregon side of the state line, known for savoury Syrah.

questions.q: Which grape is the most planted in Oregon?
questions.exp: Pinot Noir is planted far more widely than any other grape in the state. Pinot Gris leads the whites, Chardonnay is climbing, and Syrah belongs to Southern Oregon and the Rocks District.

questions.q: What share of the grapes must be grown in Oregon when a label names Oregon as the appellation?
questions.exp: Oregon requires every grape to be Oregon grown for a state label, where federal law would accept 75 per cent for a state appellation.

questions.q: Which valley holds the Applegate Valley AVA?
questions.exp: Applegate Valley is nested inside the Rogue Valley AVA in the far south of the state. Umpqua holds Elkton Oregon and Red Hill Douglas County instead.

questions.q: What minimum share of the named grape must an Oregon wine labelled Cabernet Sauvignon contain?
questions.exp: Cabernet Sauvignon is on Oregon's list of grapes blended by tradition, which may be labelled at the federal 75 per cent. Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and most other grapes must reach Oregon's 90.

regions.name: Willamette Valley (OR)
regions.summary: The Willamette Valley is Oregon's Pinot Noir country: a long, cool valley south of Portland held between the Coast Range and the Cascades, wet in winter, dry in summer, where Pinot Noir has grown since 1965 and is by far the leading grape. The AVA dates from 1983; by 2022 eleven AVAs were nested inside it, Dundee Hills, Yamhill-Carlton and Eola-Amity Hills the names a server meets most. Soil is the local argument: red volcanic Jory against marine sediment against windblown loess. Pinot Gris leads the whites, Chardonnay has climbed since the Dijon clones arrived, and the valley makes serious traditional-method sparkling wine. Oregon's label law is stricter than federal law, and the exam loves that fact.

terroir.climate: Cool and maritime at about 45 degrees north, two degrees south of Burgundy. The Pacific lies about 80 kilometres (fifty miles) west beyond the Coast Range, which takes the worst of the storms; about 1,000 millimetres (forty inches) of rain fall in a year, nearly all between November and April, and summers are dry and mild with cool nights. Harvest runs from late September into October, when autumn rain is the standing threat. The Van Duzer Corridor, a gap in the Coast Range west of Salem, draws cool ocean air across the Eola-Amity Hills every afternoon. Vintages vary more than in California.
terroir.soils: Three families, and a Willamette grower will tell you which one is under the vine. Jory is the red, iron-rich clay weathered from Columbia River basalt that covers the Dundee Hills and much of the Eola-Amity Hills; it was named Oregon's state soil in 2011. Willakenzie and its kin are marine sediments, old sandstone and siltstone lifted from the sea floor, under Yamhill-Carlton, Ribbon Ridge and McMinnville. Laurelwood is windblown loess over basalt on the north faces of the Chehalem Mountains and in the Tualatin Hills. The valley floor is Missoula flood silt and is left to other crops.
terroir.topography: The valley runs about 240 kilometres (150 miles) from the Columbia River at Portland south to beyond Eugene, about 100 kilometres (sixty miles) across at its widest, with the Coast Range to the west and the Cascades to the east. Vineyards sit on hillsides, not the floor: the volcanic Dundee Hills, the Eola and Amity hills, the Chehalem Mountains with Bald Peak their summit, and the Coast Range foothills behind McMinnville and Yamhill. Most plantings lie between about 60 and 300 metres (200 and 1,000 feet), above the old flood line and below the cold of the ridges, on south and east aspects. The northern half of the valley, Yamhill County above all, holds most of the vines.
terroir.water: The Willamette River flows north to the Columbia at Portland and drains the valley rather than moderating it; the Pacific does the moderating, through the Van Duzer Corridor and the lesser gaps of the Coast Range.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The valley's reason for being: red cherry and raspberry, forest floor and spice, silky tannin, moderate alcohol, a wine that leans towards Burgundy rather than California and ages well from the better hillsides.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: The leading white and the first Pinot Gris planted in the United States, at Eyrie in the 1960s: dry, pear and apple, a little weight, almost never oaked.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Transformed by the Dijon clones planted from the late 1980s, which ripen in time; taut, citrus and white-flower wines fermented in barrel with restraint.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: A small planting of dry and off-dry wines from the cooler sites, a survivor of the valley's first experiments.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: An occasional dry white, round and quiet, grown by a few of the older houses.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.styles: Bright, crunchy, lightly chilled reds in the Beaujolais manner from a growing handful of houses.

grapes.name: Pinot Meunier
grapes.styles: The third grape of the valley's traditional-method sparkling blends beside Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

wines.note: Red cherry, cranberry, dried rose and damp earth, silky tannin and bright acidity. Serve a touch below room temperature with duck, salmon, mushrooms or roast chicken; the valley's calling card.
The Jory soil shows as red fruit, perfume and a fine, open texture. A wine to pour against a Yamhill-Carlton bottle to show a guest what soil does.
Marine sediment gives darker fruit, black cherry and plum, with a broader, earthier frame than the Dundee Hills. Good with lamb and with anything off the grill.
Dry, pear, apple and a hint of honeysuckle, a little richer than Italian Grigio and lighter than Alsace. Chilled, with shellfish, trout or a salad course.
Lemon, green apple and wet stone, the oak quiet, the acidity keen; the best bottles are mistaken for Burgundy. Serve with crab, roast fish or a cream sauce.
Traditional-method sparkling wine from Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sometimes Meunier, aged on its lees for years: apple, brioche and fine bubbles. A natural opening glass.
Pale, dry and strawberry-scented, made by direct pressing or a short soak; chilled, for warm evenings and lighter plates.

made.viticulture: The pioneers planted on wide spacing; the generation after Drouhin's arrival in 1987 planted closer, trained on vertical shoot positioning with Guyot or cordon pruning. The first vines were Pommard and Wädenswil selections of Pinot Noir; the Dijon clones, 113, 114, 115, 667 and 777 among them, came from the late 1980s and gave earlier ripening and a different stamp. Phylloxera was found in the valley in 1990 and most vineyards went onto rootstock through the following decades, though some older blocks stand on their own roots. Winter rain fills the soil and many hillside sites are dry farmed. The hazards are the autumn rains that can arrive during harvest, botrytis and powdery mildew in a damp year, frost in low pockets, birds, and in recent summers smoke from forest fires. The valley is a stronghold of organic and biodynamic farming and of LIVE certification, and growers watch aspect and elevation closely: too low and the site is cold and frosty, too high and the fruit will not ripen.
made.winemaking: Pinot Noir is made in the Burgundian manner adapted to a cool, wet place: sorting, a share of whole clusters that varies house by house, a cold soak, fermentation in small open vessels with punch-downs, often with native yeasts, then ten to eighteen months in French barrels of which a modest share, commonly a fifth to two fifths, is new. Chaptalisation is sometimes needed in a cool year and is permitted. Pinot Gris is pressed and fermented cool in stainless steel, dry, and bottled young; Chardonnay since the Dijon clones is barrel fermented with full malolactic conversion and restrained new oak. Sparkling wine is traditional method, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with some Meunier, aged on lees for several years, a style Argyle established in Dundee from 1987.

law.classification: The Willamette Valley AVA was approved in 1983 and, like every AVA, states origin only: no grape, yield, method or quality rule comes with the name. Oregon adds its own floors. A varietal wine must hold 90 per cent of the named grape, against the federal 75, with a listed group of traditionally blended grapes, Cabernet Sauvignon among them, allowed at 75. A wine naming the Willamette Valley or one of its nested AVAs must hold 95 per cent from that area, against the federal 85, and a wine labelled Oregon must be Oregon grapes entirely. Under a statute of 2019, in force for labels from 1 January 2023, a label that names a nested AVA must also carry the words Willamette Valley. Estate Bottled is the federal term and means every grape from the winery's own or controlled vineyards inside the AVA, the wine made and bottled on site. Reserve, Old Vine and Barrel Select carry no legal meaning.
tiers: The state appellation: every grape Oregon grown.
The AVA of 1983: 95 per cent of the grapes from inside it under Oregon law.

Chehalem Mountains, Dundee Hills, Eola-Amity Hills, Laurelwood District, Lower Long Tom, McMinnville, Mount Pisgah (Polk County), Ribbon Ridge, Tualatin Hills, Van Duzer Corridor and Yamhill-Carlton: 95 per cent from the named area, and the words Willamette Valley alongside.
A named vineyard, the house's own claim, no legal tier; the grapes still meet the AVA rule.
labels: The valley AVA; also the words required beside any nested AVA name since 2023.
Federal: grapes from vineyards the winery owns or controls in the AVA, wine made and bottled on the premises.
No legal meaning; a house's own word for a selection.
Oregon nearly always says Gris rather than Grigio; the wine is dry and unoaked.
The Pacific Northwest's sustainability certification for vineyards and wineries.

places.name: Dundee Hills
places.note: The valley's first famous hill, an AVA since 2005: red Jory clay over basalt above the town of Dundee, where Eyrie settled in 1966 and Drouhin bought land in 1987. Red-fruited, perfumed, fine-boned Pinot Noir; the exam's first Willamette name after the valley itself.

places.name: Yamhill-Carlton
places.note: A horseshoe of Coast Range foothills around the towns of Yamhill and Carlton, approved in 2005 on ancient marine sediment, Willakenzie and its cousins. Darker, broader Pinot Noir than the Dundee Hills, black cherry and earth. Carlton's main street is lined with tasting rooms.

places.name: Eola-Amity Hills
places.note: A volcanic ridge north-west of Salem, approved in 2006, directly in the path of the Van Duzer Corridor. The afternoon wind cools the fruit and thickens the skins: firmer, spicier, higher-acid Pinot Noir than Dundee's. Cristom and the Seven Springs vineyard are here.

places.name: Chehalem Mountains
places.note: The valley's highest ridge, Bald Peak its 498-metre (1,633-foot) summit, north of Newberg, approved in 2006. The only nested AVA with all three soil families, basalt, marine sediment and Laurelwood loess, so its wines vary face by face. Ribbon Ridge and the Laurelwood District sit inside it.

places.name: Ribbon Ridge
places.note: The smallest of the older nested AVAs, approved in 2005 on a sedimentary ridge within the Chehalem Mountains north-west of Newberg. Dark-fruited, structured Pinot Noir; Beaux Frères is the famous name.

places.name: McMinnville
places.note: The Coast Range foothills west of the town of McMinnville, approved in 2005: uplifted marine sediment and basalt, shallow soils, and a site that catches the Van Duzer wind. Dark fruit and firm structure. The town hosts the International Pinot Noir Celebration each summer, begun in 1987.

places.name: Van Duzer Corridor
places.note: The gap in the Coast Range itself, approved as an AVA in 2019 west of Salem: the coolest, windiest ground in the northern valley, planted to Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris of high acidity on marine sediment.

places.name: Laurelwood District
places.note: Approved in 2020 inside the Chehalem Mountains, named for the Laurelwood loess, windblown silt over basalt on the north and east faces of the ridge. Lighter, aromatic Pinot Noir and fine Pinot Gris.

places.name: Tualatin Hills
places.note: The northern end of the valley near Forest Grove, approved in 2020, among the wettest and coolest of the nested AVAs, with Laurelwood loess under most of its vines and the Tualatin River below.

places.name: Lower Long Tom
places.note: The first nested AVA of the southern valley, approved in 2021 north-west of Eugene, towards Corvallis, on shallow sedimentary Bellpine soils along the Long Tom River; Pinot Noir of ripe, dark fruit from a warmer, drier corner than the north.

places.name: Mount Pisgah, Polk County, Oregon
places.note: The eleventh nested AVA, approved in 2022: a small hill south-west of Salem whose marine sediments were lifted by a volcanic intrusion, with Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris on its slopes. Its full legal name carries the county and the state.

places.name: Newberg, Dundee and Carlton
places.note: The three towns of the northern valley a server will hear: Newberg below the Chehalem Mountains, Dundee under its red hills, Carlton at the heart of Yamhill-Carlton. McMinnville between them is the valley's wine capital.

producers.name: The Eyrie Vineyards
producers.why: Planted the valley's first Pinot Noir and the country's first Pinot Gris from 1965, and its 1975 South Block Reserve put Oregon on the map in Paris in 1979.

producers.name: Domaine Drouhin Oregon
producers.why: The Beaune house of Joseph Drouhin bought Dundee Hills land in 1987, the clearest vote of confidence Burgundy ever gave the New World.

producers.name: Argyle
producers.why: Dundee's traditional-method sparkling house since 1987, and a reference for Willamette Brut as well as still Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

producers.name: Bergström Wines
producers.why: A Newberg family estate farmed biodynamically, with single-vineyard Pinot Noir across several nested AVAs.

producers.name: Beaux Frères
producers.why: The Ribbon Ridge estate that made the tiny AVA famous, dense and polished Pinot Noir from biodynamic vines.

producers.name: Cristom Vineyards
producers.why: The Eola-Amity Hills reference, whole-cluster Pinot Noir from named estate vineyards in the Van Duzer wind.

producers.name: Ken Wright Cellars
producers.why: A Carlton house built on single-vineyard Pinot Noir bottlings that taught the trade to taste the nested AVAs side by side.

producers.name: Adelsheim Vineyard
producers.why: A Chehalem Mountains pioneer of 1971 and a long-standing voice in the valley's clonal and AVA work.

producers.name: Ponzi Vineyards
producers.why: Planted in 1970 in the Chehalem Mountains foothills; one of the four founding families with Eyrie, Erath and Adelsheim.

producers.name: Erath
producers.why: A Dundee Hills pioneer with its first vintage in 1972, now a large house whose Pinot Noir is on many lists.

producers.name: Sokol Blosser
producers.why: Dundee Hills since 1971, an early organic estate and an early name in Oregon Pinot Gris.

producers.name: Domaine Serene
producers.why: A Dundee Hills estate from 1989 whose Pinot Noir and Chardonnay carry the valley's luxury end.

producers.name: Evening Land Vineyards
producers.why: Long associated with the Seven Springs vineyard in the Eola-Amity Hills, a reference site for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Résonance
producers.why: The Oregon estate of the Burgundy house Louis Jadot, begun with a Yamhill-Carlton vineyard bought in 2013, the second great Burgundian arrival.

exam: Name the founding: Eyrie planted Pinot Noir in 1965, the AVA came in 1983, Drouhin arrived in 1987.
Hold the three soils and their hills: Jory on the Dundee Hills, marine sediment under Yamhill-Carlton and Ribbon Ridge, Laurelwood loess on the Chehalem Mountains and Tualatin Hills.
Know the Van Duzer Corridor as the gap that cools the Eola-Amity Hills, and since 2019 an AVA in its own right.
List the six older nested AVAs of 2005 and 2006 before the five newer ones.
Carry Oregon's percentages into every question: 90 varietal, 95 AVA, 100 Oregon.
Pair the grape and the style: Pinot Noir red-fruited and silky, Pinot Gris dry and unoaked, Chardonnay from Dijon clones, Brut by the traditional method.
traps: Jory is volcanic and red; Willakenzie is marine sediment. Swap them and the Dundee Hills question is lost.
Willamette rhymes with dammit: wil-LAM-it, never will-a-MET.
The valley is cool and wet, but the summers are dry; harvest rain, not summer rain, is the hazard.
Ribbon Ridge and the Laurelwood District lie inside the Chehalem Mountains AVA; no other nested AVA holds another.
Oregon's Pinot Gris is dry and fuller than Italian Grigio; the label almost never says Grigio here.
Domaine Drouhin Oregon is a Burgundian house's estate, not a Burgundy import; the wine is Dundee Hills fruit.
The Columbia Gorge and Southern Oregon are not in the Willamette Valley; a Syrah or Tempranillo question points south or east.

cards.f: Willamette Valley AVA: year, and its boundaries
cards.b: Approved in 1983. The Coast Range west, the Cascades east, the Columbia River north, the Calapooya Mountains south of Eugene; about 240 kilometres (150 miles) long.

cards.f: Jory soil: what it is and where
cards.b: Red, iron-rich clay weathered from basalt, the Dundee Hills' signature and Oregon's state soil since 2011; also much of the Eola-Amity Hills.

cards.f: Willakenzie soil: what it is and where
cards.b: Ancient marine sediment, sandstone and siltstone, under Yamhill-Carlton, Ribbon Ridge and McMinnville; darker, earthier Pinot Noir.

cards.f: The six older nested AVAs and their years
cards.b: Dundee Hills, Yamhill-Carlton, McMinnville and Ribbon Ridge in 2005; Chehalem Mountains and Eola-Amity Hills in 2006.
Van Duzer Corridor 2019; Laurelwood District and Tualatin Hills 2020; Lower Long Tom 2021; Mount Pisgah, Polk County, Oregon 2022.

cards.f: The Van Duzer Corridor: what and why it matters
cards.b: A gap in the Coast Range west of Salem that funnels cool Pacific air across the Eola-Amity Hills each afternoon; an AVA itself since 2019.

cards.f: Eyrie's 1975 Pinot Noir: why it matters
cards.b: The South Block Reserve placed among the top Pinot Noirs at a Paris tasting in 1979 and nearly beat Drouhin's own Burgundy in a 1980 rematch; Drouhin came to Oregon in 1987.

cards.f: The three grapes of a Willamette Brut
cards.b: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier, traditional method, aged on lees; Argyle's house style since 1987.
A label naming a Willamette nested AVA must also carry the words Willamette Valley, with 95 per cent of the grapes from the named area.

questions.q: Which soil series is the red volcanic clay of the Dundee Hills?
questions.exp: Jory is the iron-rich clay weathered from basalt that covers the Dundee Hills. Willakenzie and Bellpine are marine sediments; Laurelwood is windblown loess.

questions.q: In which year was the Willamette Valley AVA approved?
questions.exp: The valley became an AVA in 1983, eighteen years after Eyrie's first Pinot Noir vines and four years before Drouhin arrived.

questions.q: Which gap in the Coast Range funnels cool Pacific air across the Eola-Amity Hills?
questions.exp: The Van Duzer Corridor west of Salem lets ocean air into the valley each afternoon, cooling the Eola-Amity Hills; it became an AVA of its own in 2019.

questions.q: Which nested AVA lies entirely inside the Chehalem Mountains AVA?
questions.exp: Ribbon Ridge, approved in 2005, is a small sedimentary ridge within the Chehalem Mountains; the Laurelwood District of 2020 is the other. The rest stand alone.

questions.q: Which grape leads the white plantings of the Willamette Valley?
questions.exp: Pinot Gris, first planted at Eyrie in the 1960s, is the leading white; Chardonnay has risen since the Dijon clones, and Riesling and Pinot Blanc are small.

questions.q: What minimum share of Pinot Noir must a Willamette Valley wine labelled Pinot Noir contain?
questions.exp: Oregon sets the varietal minimum at 90 per cent for Pinot Noir and most grapes, above the federal 75; only a listed group of blended grapes may use 75.

questions.q: Which house's 1975 Pinot Noir placed among the best at the Paris tasting of 1979?
questions.exp: Eyrie's 1975 South Block Reserve was the wine; the showing led Joseph Drouhin to a rematch in 1980 and to Oregon in 1987. The other three are fellow pioneers.

questions.q: Which Beaune négociant bought land in Oregon's Dundee Hills in 1987?
questions.exp: Joseph Drouhin of Beaune bought the land in 1987 and made the first vintage of Domaine Drouhin Oregon in 1988, the first great Burgundian investment in the valley.
